es: Leer un artículo de opinión y analizarlo: identificar la tesis, la postura y las concesiones, detectar suposiciones y apoyar cada inferencia en una pista del texto.

teaching.en: The thesis is the main idea: the writer argues that cities should be slower.
teaching.es: La tesis es la idea principal: el autor sostiene que las ciudades deberían ser más lentas.
teaching.explanationEs: Thesis = tesis. Suele estar al principio o al final; busca verbos como argue, claim o believe.
segments: The thesis is the main idea: the
writer argues that cities should be slower.
teaching.audioText: The thesis is the main idea: the writer argues that cities should be slower.

teaching.en: Admittedly, slower traffic may annoy some drivers, but the writer still argues for it.
teaching.es: Es cierto que el tráfico más lento puede molestar a algunos conductores, pero el autor aun así lo defiende.
teaching.explanationEs: Admittedly concede un punto al otro lado; lo que el autor defiende viene después de but.
segments: Admittedly, slower traffic may annoy some drivers,
but the writer still argues for it.
teaching.audioText: Admittedly, slower traffic may annoy some drivers, but the writer still argues for it.

teaching.en: A counterargument is the other side's best point, and a strong writer answers it.
teaching.es: Un contraargumento es el mejor punto del otro lado, y un autor sólido lo responde.
teaching.explanationEs: Si el autor no responde al contraargumento, su tesis queda más débil.
segments: A counterargument is the other side's best
point, and a strong writer answers it.
teaching.audioText: A counterargument is the other side's best point, and a strong writer answers it.

teaching.en: The writer assumes that shorter journeys are always better, but that assumption is never proved.
teaching.es: El autor da por hecho que los trayectos cortos siempre son mejores, pero esa suposición nunca se demuestra.
teaching.explanationEs: Assumption = suposición: una idea que el texto da por cierta sin pruebas. Palabras como always y obviously la delatan.
segments: The writer assumes that shorter journeys are always
better, but that assumption is never proved.
teaching.audioText: The writer assumes that shorter journeys are always better, but that assumption is never proved.

teaching.en: If the writer says 'even parents now walk to school', we can infer that walking was rare before.
teaching.es: Si el autor dice «ahora hasta los padres van andando al colegio», podemos inferir que antes era raro.
teaching.explanationEs: Infer = deducir algo que el texto no dice pero apoya. Siempre hay una pista: aquí even y now.
segments: If the writer says 'even parents now walk to
school', we can infer that walking was rare before.
teaching.audioText: If the writer says 'even parents now walk to school', we can infer that walking was rare before.

teaching.en: A rhetorical question, such as 'Who wants noisy streets?', shows stance but proves nothing.
teaching.es: Una pregunta retórica, como «¿Quién quiere calles ruidosas?», muestra postura pero no demuestra nada.
teaching.explanationEs: No espera respuesta: sirve para persuadir, no para aportar evidencia.
segments: A rhetorical question, such as 'Who wants
noisy streets?', shows stance but proves nothing.
teaching.audioText: A rhetorical question, such as 'Who wants noisy streets?', shows stance but proves nothing.

prompt.es: ¿Cuál es la tesis del autor en este fragmento?

choices.text: Streets should be designed for people, not only for cars.
Cars should be faster in the city.
The city has no streets.

feedback.es: El autor pregunta si las calles están pensadas para las personas y no solo para los coches: su tesis es que deberían diseñarse para la gente.

hint.es: La tesis responde a la pregunta «¿qué defiende el autor?».

origin.text: Our city has spent fifty years designing streets for cars. It is time to ask whether those streets are designed for people.

prompt.es: Completa: «Es cierto que algunos conductores protestarán, pero…»

feedback.es: Admittedly concede un punto al otro lado antes del but y muestra que el autor conoce la objeción.

hint.es: Es el adverbio que reconoce un punto contrario antes de but.

origin.text: ___, some drivers will complain, but the benefits are greater.

prompt.es: ¿Qué se puede inferir de este fragmento?

choices.text: Parents dislike walking.
Walking to school was not common before.
Schools are closing.

feedback.es: Even y now marcan un cambio sorprendente: si hasta los padres van ahora andando, antes no era habitual.

hint.es: Fíjate en even y now: marcan un cambio respecto al pasado.

origin.text: Even parents now walk their children to school.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué recurso usa el autor.

choices.text: A statistic that proves his thesis.
A concession to the other side.
A rhetorical question that expresses his stance.

feedback.es: La pregunta no espera respuesta («Nobody.») y expresa la postura del autor sin aportar pruebas: es una pregunta retórica.

origin.audio: Who wants noisy streets, dirty air and unsafe crossings? Nobody.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada término de análisis con su definición.

pairs.es: Lo que el autor defiende
El mejor punto del otro lado
Lo que se da por cierto sin probarlo
Deducir algo a partir de una pista

feedback.es: Cada término nombra una pieza del argumento: lo que se defiende, la objeción contraria, lo que se da por cierto y lo que se deduce.

pairs.es: Lo que el autor defiende
El mejor punto del otro lado
Lo que se da por cierto sin probarlo
Deducir algo a partir de una pista

prompt.es: Ordena: «El autor sostiene que las ciudades deberían ser más lentas.»

answer.text: The writer argues that cities should be slower

feedback.es: Argue + that + oración: el verbo argue introduce la tesis del autor.

prompt.es: ¿Qué hace el autor con la objeción de los críticos?

choices.text: He concedes a small point and then answers it.
He ignores the objection completely.
He agrees and changes his thesis.

feedback.es: Reconoce que el límite más bajo retrasa algo los trayectos y responde con un argumento más fuerte (la seguridad): concede un punto y lo contesta.

origin.text: Critics say a lower speed limit will make journeys longer. It is true that a few journeys will take two minutes more. But a safe crossing for a child is worth two minutes.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué opina el autor del ayuntamiento.

choices.text: He is enthusiastic: the council is fast.
He is unhappy: the promise was not kept.
He is neutral: he gives no opinion.

feedback.es: El autor recuerda que la promesa era para junio y que en octubre los conductores siguen esperando: es una crítica, no un elogio ni una postura neutral.

origin.audio: The council promised quiet streets by June. It is now October, and the drivers are still waiting for the new signs.

prompt.es: ¿Qué suposición no demostrada hace el autor?

choices.text: That the rules are new.
That the city is quiet.
That everyone prefers a slower city.

feedback.es: «Obviously» y «everyone» dan por hecho que a todos les gusta una ciudad lenta, sin ninguna prueba. Que las reglas sean nuevas o que la ciudad sea tranquila no es la suposición.

origin.text: Everyone obviously prefers a slower city, so the new rules will be popular.

prompt.es: Completa tres notas de análisis: tesis, concesión e inferencia.

feedback.es: Argues introduce la tesis, admits reconoce el punto contrario (la concesión) e infer señala una deducción apoyada en una pista.

sentences: The writer ___ that cities should be slower.
The writer ___ that the lower limit may annoy some drivers, but he still defends it.
From the word 'still' we can ___ that the signs are late.

prompt.es: ¿Qué se puede inferir de la expresión «a first step»?

choices.text: That more changes will probably follow.
That the limit will be removed.
That the mayor dislikes the limit.

feedback.es: Llamar «first step» al nuevo límite da a entender que se esperan más cambios después; no dice que se vaya a retirar ni que la alcaldesa lo rechace.

origin.text: The mayor calls the new limit 'a first step'.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige cuál es la postura final del autor.

choices.text: He changes his mind and supports the drivers.
He accepts the drivers' feeling but keeps his position.
He refuses to give an opinion.

feedback.es: El autor concede que los conductores se sienten castigados, pero añade «even so» y mantiene su posición: concede sin cambiar de tesis.

origin.audio: I accept that drivers feel punished. Even so, I still believe that the lower limit is right.

prompt.es: Completa: «Una pregunta retórica no espera respuesta.»

feedback.es: Una pregunta retórica se hace para expresar postura o persuadir, no para recibir una respuesta.

origin.text: A ___ question does not expect an answer.

es: Revisar un borrador y corregir seis problemas de registro, cohesión y matiz, cambiando lo vago por datos exactos y las afirmaciones exageradas por otras ajustadas.

teaching.en: In a message to the director, a formal register starts with Dear Ms Lopez, not Hi all.
teaching.es: En un mensaje a la directora, un registro formal empieza con Dear Ms Lopez, no con Hi all.
teaching.explanationEs: Register: el saludo y las palabras deben encajar con quien lee.
segments: In a message to the director, a formal register
starts with Dear Ms Lopez, not Hi all.
teaching.audioText: In a message to the director, a formal register starts with Dear Ms Lopez, not Hi all.

teaching.en: A strong claim can overstate the evidence: 'many students seem to dislike it' is more precise than 'everyone hates it'.
teaching.es: Una afirmación fuerte puede exagerar la evidencia: «many students seem to dislike it» es más preciso que «everyone hates it».
teaching.explanationEs: Overstate = exagerar. Sustituye todos/nadie por many/some y añade seem.
segments: A strong claim can overstate the evidence: 'many students seem
to dislike it' is more precise than 'everyone hates it'.
teaching.audioText: A strong claim can overstate the evidence: 'many students seem to dislike it' is more precise than 'everyone hates it'.

teaching.en: A linker such as however or so gives the text cohesion.
teaching.es: Un conector como however o so da cohesión al texto.
teaching.explanationEs: Cohesion: las frases cortas y sueltas se unen con un linker (so, however, although).
segments: A linker such as however or
so gives the text cohesion.
teaching.audioText: A linker such as however or so gives the text cohesion.

teaching.en: Vague words like soon should become exact details, such as by Friday.
teaching.es: Las palabras vagas como soon deben convertirse en datos exactos, como by Friday.
teaching.explanationEs: Vague = impreciso. Un plazo con fecha es más útil que un adverbio.
segments: Vague words like soon should become
exact details, such as by Friday.
teaching.audioText: Vague words like soon should become exact details, such as by Friday.

teaching.en: To hedge a claim, add seem, may or appear: the price appears to have risen.
teaching.es: Para matizar una afirmación, añade seem, may o appear: el precio parece haber subido.
teaching.explanationEs: Hedge = matizar. Seem to / appear to + verbo suavizan sin perder información.
segments: To hedge a claim, add seem, may or
appear: the price appears to have risen.
teaching.audioText: To hedge a claim, add seem, may or appear: the price appears to have risen.

teaching.en: After you revise a draft, read it aloud and ask whether each change makes it more precise.
teaching.es: Después de revisar un borrador, léelo en voz alta y pregúntate si cada cambio lo hace más preciso.
teaching.explanationEs: Revise = revisar con cambios reales: cada cambio debe mejorar el registro, la cohesión o el matiz.
segments: After you revise a draft, read it aloud and
ask whether each change makes it more precise.
teaching.audioText: After you revise a draft, read it aloud and ask whether each change makes it more precise.

prompt.es: ¿Qué problema tiene este saludo al escribir a la directora?

choices.text: Cohesion: it has no linkers.
Register: it is too casual for the director.
Hedging: it is too cautious.

feedback.es: Un saludo informal como «Hi all!» no encaja con un mensaje a la directora: es un problema de registro. No falta ningún conector ni hay exceso de cautela.

hint.es: Piensa a quién va dirigido el mensaje.

origin.text: Draft: Hi all! The director must read this today.

prompt.es: Completa: «A muchos estudiantes parece no gustarles el nuevo menú.»

feedback.es: Seem to + verbo matiza la afirmación: no dice que todos lo odian, sino que parece que a muchos no les gusta.

hint.es: Es el verbo que atenúa: «parece que», no «es seguro que».

origin.text: Many students ___ to dislike the new menu.

prompt.es: ¿Qué cambio sustituye lo vago por un dato exacto?

choices.text: We will ask the director soon.
We will ask the director later.
We will ask the director by Friday.

feedback.es: «By Friday» da un plazo concreto; soon y later son adverbios vagos que no dicen cuándo.

hint.es: Un dato exacto es un día, no un adverbio.

origin.text: Draft: We will ask the director soon.

prompt.es: Ordena: «El menú es nuevo y a los estudiantes parece gustarles.»

answer.text: The menu is new and students seem to like it
accepted: The menu is new and students seem to like it
The menu is new and students appear to like it

feedback.es: El conector and une las dos ideas y seem to matiza la segunda: cohesión y matiz en una sola frase.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué dos mejoras tiene la versión editada.

choices.text: A linker joins the ideas, and seem softens the claim.
The register becomes formal, and a date is added.
The ideas are cut, and the claim is stronger.

feedback.es: La versión editada une las frases con and (cohesión) y suaviza con seem to (matiz). No cambia el registro ni añade fechas.

origin.audio: Before the edit: The menu is new. Students like it. After the edit: The menu is new, and students seem to like it.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada área de revisión con su pregunta de comprobación.

pairs.es: ¿El saludo y las palabras encajan con el lector?
¿Los conectores enlazan las frases?
¿La afirmación fuerte se ajusta con seem o may?
¿Hay datos exactos en lugar de soon?

feedback.es: Cada área tiene una pregunta propia: el registro mira al lector, la cohesión a los conectores, el matiz a la fuerza de la afirmación y lo vago a los datos.

pairs.es: ¿El saludo y las palabras encajan con el lector?
¿Los conectores enlazan las frases?
¿La afirmación fuerte se ajusta con seem o may?
¿Hay datos exactos en lugar de soon?

prompt.es: ¿Qué lista resume los problemas principales del borrador?

choices.text: A formal greeting, too many hedges and long sentences.
A casual greeting, overstated claims and a vague time.
A missing thanks, wrong tenses and no title.

feedback.es: El borrador abre con «Hi all», exagera con «everyone hates it» y «obviously» y deja un plazo vago con «soon». El agradecimiento sí aparece al final.

origin.text: Hi all. The school food is terrible and everyone hates it. The new menu is obviously better. Students like it. The price went up. The cooks say they are sorry. We must change the menu now. The director must read this today. We will ask her soon. Last week, two students were ill after lunch. The parents are angry. Nobody wants to wait in a long line. Thank you.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué dos áreas mejoró el editor.

choices.text: Cohesion and vague details.
Hedging and vague details.
Register and hedging.

feedback.es: Cambiar Hi all por Dear Ms Lopez mejora el registro, y sustituir «everyone hates it» por «many students seem to dislike it» mejora el matiz.

origin.audio: I changed the greeting to Dear Ms Lopez, and I replaced everyone hates it with many students seem to dislike it.

prompt.es: Completa tres ediciones: conector, plazo exacto y matiz.

feedback.es: However abre el contraste, by marca un plazo exacto («by Monday at the latest») y appears to matiza un dato que no es seguro.

sentences: The price rose; ___, students still seem to like the menu.
Please send your reply ___ Monday at the latest.

prompt.es: Reescribe en un solo mensaje formal: saludo, matiz, conector y plazo exacto.

answer.text: Dear Ms Lopez, many students seem to dislike the school food, so we will ask you to review the menu by Friday.
accepted: Dear Ms Lopez, many students seem to dislike the school food, so we will ask you to review the menu by Friday.
Dear Ms Lopez, it appears that many students dislike the food, and we will ask you to change the menu by Friday.
Dear Ms Lopez, some students seem to dislike the school food; therefore, we will ask you to review the menu before Friday.

feedback.es: Un mensaje editado abre con saludo formal, matiza «todos odian» con seem to y many, une las ideas con un conector y fija un plazo exacto.

origin.text: Borrador: «Hi all. Everyone hates the food. We will ask soon.» Reescríbelo como un solo mensaje a la directora, la señora Lopez: saludo formal, matiz en «todos odian», un conector y el plazo exacto (el viernes).

prompt.es: ¿Qué edición aporta cohesión al borrador?

choices.text: The cooks say they are sorry, and they will change the menu.
The cooks say they are sorry. They will change the menu.
The cooks, sorry, change menu.

feedback.es: El conector and une las dos ideas en una sola frase; la versión original las deja sueltas y la tercera elimina palabras sin aportar cohesión.

origin.text: Draft: The cooks say they are sorry. They will change the menu.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué mejoró el editor.

choices.text: He made the register more casual.
He softened an overstated claim and compared it with a fact.
He added a linker between two sentences.

feedback.es: El editor cambió «obviously too high» por «appears to be higher than last year»: suavizó una afirmación exagerada y la apoyó con una comparación.

origin.audio: The draft says the price is obviously too high. The editor changed it to: the price appears to be higher than last year.

prompt.es: Completa: «Antes de enviarlo, voy a revisar el borrador.»

feedback.es: Revise significa revisar con cambios reales; después de revisar el borrador se lee en voz alta para comprobar el tono.

origin.text: Before I send it, I will ___ the draft.

es: Sintetizar la información de un audio y de un texto: comparar lo que coincide, señalar las discrepancias y cerrar con una conclusión.

teaching.en: According to the radio report, the library closes in June, whereas the newspaper says it closes in July.
teaching.es: Según el informe de la radio, la biblioteca cierra en junio, mientras que el periódico dice que cierra en julio.
teaching.explanationEs: Whereas contrasta dos fuentes: cada una con su dato, en una sola frase.
segments: According to the radio report, the library closes in
June, whereas the newspaper says it closes in July.
teaching.audioText: According to the radio report, the library closes in June, whereas the newspaper says it closes in July.

teaching.en: Both sources agree that the library is too small.
teaching.es: Las dos fuentes coinciden en que la biblioteca es demasiado pequeña.
teaching.explanationEs: Both + fuentes en plural + verbo sin -s: señala una coincidencia.
segments: Both sources agree that the
library is too small.
teaching.audioText: Both sources agree that the library is too small.

teaching.en: Likewise, the radio figure and the newspaper figure show that visits fell last year.
teaching.es: Del mismo modo, la cifra de la radio y la del periódico muestran que las visitas cayeron el año pasado.
teaching.explanationEs: Likewise añade otra coincidencia. Figure = cifra o dato numérico.
segments: Likewise, the radio figure and the newspaper
figure show that visits fell last year.
teaching.audioText: Likewise, the radio figure and the newspaper figure show that visits fell last year.

teaching.en: There is a discrepancy: the radio says 400 visitors, but the newspaper gives 300.
teaching.es: Hay una discrepancia: la radio dice 400 visitantes, pero el periódico da 300.
teaching.explanationEs: Discrepancy = diferencia entre datos. Se nombra y luego se explica (¿quién habla? ¿cuándo?).
segments: There is a discrepancy: the radio says
400 visitors, but the newspaper gives 300.
teaching.audioText: There is a discrepancy: the radio says 400 visitors, but the newspaper gives 300.

teaching.en: The radio source is the library manager, so her figure may be more exact.
teaching.es: La fuente de la radio es la directora de la biblioteca, así que su cifra puede ser más exacta.
teaching.explanationEs: Evaluar la fuente: quién habla y qué sabe. Es parte de una buena síntesis.
segments: The radio source is the library manager,
so her figure may be more exact.
teaching.audioText: The radio source is the library manager, so her figure may be more exact.

teaching.en: Overall, the two sources agree on the problem, but they differ on the date.
teaching.es: En conjunto, las dos fuentes coinciden en el problema, pero difieren en la fecha.
teaching.explanationEs: Overall abre la conclusión: resume coincidencias y diferencias en una frase.
segments: Overall, the two sources agree on the
problem, but they differ on the date.
teaching.audioText: Overall, the two sources agree on the problem, but they differ on the date.

prompt.es: ¿Qué relación hay entre las dos fuentes sobre la apertura de la piscina?

choices.text: They agree on the date.
They do not mention the date.
They show a discrepancy about the date.

feedback.es: La radio dice el 1 de mayo y el artículo el 15 de mayo: los datos no coinciden, así que hay una discrepancia sobre la fecha.

origin.text: Radio: The pool opens on 1 May. Article: The pool opens on 15 May.

prompt.es: Completa: «La radio dice junio, mientras que el periódico dice julio.»

feedback.es: Whereas contrasta dos datos de dos fuentes distintas en una sola frase.

hint.es: Es el conector de contraste que equivale a «mientras que».

origin.text: The radio says June, ___ the newspaper says July.

prompt.es: ¿Qué frase de síntesis compara correctamente las dos fuentes?

choices.text: According to the radio, 400 people visited, whereas the article gives 300.
The radio and the article say 400 people visited.
According to the article, 400 people visited, and the radio says 300.

feedback.es: Cada cifra va con su fuente y el conector whereas marca el contraste. Las otras dos mezclan o invierten los datos.

hint.es: Cada cifra debe ir con su fuente.

origin.text: Radio: 400 visitors. Article: 300 visitors.

prompt.es: Escucha, lee y elige cómo se relacionan las dos fuentes.

choices.text: They agree on the number.
They show a discrepancy in the number.
They give the same date.

feedback.es: El audio dice doscientos niños y el periódico doscientos cincuenta: los datos no coinciden, hay una discrepancia en la cifra.

origin.audio: The manager says two hundred children joined the club this year.
origin.text: Newspaper: Two hundred and fifty children joined the club this year.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada conector o término con su función en la síntesis.

pairs.es: Las dos fuentes coinciden
Contrasta dos datos
Diferencia entre datos de dos fuentes
Conclusión que resume

feedback.es: Cada término cumple una función: coincidencia, contraste, diferencia entre datos y conclusión.

pairs.es: Las dos fuentes coinciden
Contrasta dos datos
Diferencia entre datos de dos fuentes
Conclusión que resume

prompt.es: Ordena: «Las dos fuentes coinciden en la cifra, pero no en la fecha.»

answer.text: The two sources agree on the figure but not on the date

feedback.es: Agree on introduce el punto de coincidencia y but not on señala la diferencia: la coincidencia y la discrepancia caben en una sola frase.

prompt.es: Escucha, lee y elige en qué discrepan las dos fuentes.

choices.text: In the number of daily passengers.
In who runs the bus company.
In the start date of the new bus line.

feedback.es: El portavoz dice que la línea empieza en septiembre y el periódico dice octubre: esa es la discrepancia. Las dos fuentes calculan unos tres mil pasajeros al día.

origin.audio: The council spokesperson says the new bus line will carry about three thousand passengers a day from September.
origin.text: Newspaper: The new bus line starts in October. The transport company expects about three thousand passengers a day.

prompt.es: Escucha, lee y elige qué añade el audio que no dice el texto.

choices.text: That the paths stay open in winter.
That the lake is closed in winter.
That the lake opens in November.

feedback.es: El sitio web solo informa del cierre del lago de noviembre a marzo; el audio añade que los senderos siguen abiertos todo el año.

origin.audio: The park guide says the lake is closed in winter, but the paths stay open all year.
origin.text: Website: The lake is closed from November to March.

prompt.es: Completa la síntesis: contraste, coincidencia y conclusión.

feedback.es: However abre el contraste entre las dos cifras, agree marca la coincidencia y Overall abre la conclusión.

sentences: According to the radio, 60 people came. ___, the newspaper says 80.
The two sources ___ that attendance fell.
___, the main problem is the same.

prompt.es: Escucha la radio, lee el artículo y escribe una síntesis comparando las dos fuentes.

answer.text: According to the radio, the playground will open in May, whereas the article says June. Both sources agree that it will cost about two hundred thousand pounds. However, only the article mentions that some neighbours worry about the noise. Overall, the sources agree on the cost but differ on the opening date.
accepted: According to the radio, the playground will open in May, whereas the article says June. Both sources agree that it will cost about two hundred thousand pounds. However, only the article mentions that some neighbours worry about the noise. Overall, the sources agree on the cost but differ on the opening date.

The radio and the article agree that the playground will cost about two hundred thousand pounds. There is a discrepancy about the date: the radio gives May, while the article gives June. In addition, only the article reports that some neighbours are worried about the noise. Overall, the main difference is the opening date.

feedback.es: Una buena síntesis compara en un párrafo: cada fuente con su dato, lo que coincide, lo que solo dice una fuente y una conclusión.

origin.text: Article: The council confirms that the playground will open in June. It will cost about two hundred thousand pounds. Some neighbours worry about the noise.
origin.audio: The mayor says the new playground will open in May, and it will cost two hundred thousand pounds. Local families welcome the idea.

prompt.es: Escucha, lee y elige qué datos coinciden.

choices.text: The length of the exam.
The day of the exam.
The room of the exam.

feedback.es: Ambas fuentes dicen que el examen es el martes; la duración no coincide (dos horas frente a noventa minutos).

origin.audio: The teacher says the exam is on Tuesday and lasts two hours.
origin.text: School website: The exam is on Tuesday and lasts ninety minutes.

prompt.es: ¿Qué síntesis es más completa?

choices.text: Both sources say profits fell.
Source A says sales fell, but Source B says they rose.
Both sources say sales rose ten per cent, and only Source B adds that profits fell.

feedback.es: La primera recoge lo que coincide (las ventas subieron un diez por ciento) y lo que solo dice la fuente B (los beneficios bajaron). Las otras inventan datos.

origin.text: Source A: Sales rose by ten per cent. Source B: Sales rose by ten per cent, but profits fell.

prompt.es: Completa: «Del mismo modo, las dos cifras muestran una caída.»

prompt.es: Responde al dilema como si hablaras dos minutos y contesta a la pregunta inesperada.

answer.text: To begin with, I would accept the sponsor, because our club needs new equipment and the school cannot pay for it. For instance, the nets are broken, and the balls are old. On balance, I think the benefits outweigh the risks, although I see the dilemma: the café sells sweet drinks, and our club is about health. That said, I would set two conditions. First, the café must also sell water and fruit at our events. Second, the sponsor cannot decide anything about the team. As for your question about the logo, that is a fair point. Let me think for a moment. I would accept a small logo on the shirts, provided that the players agree and the logo stays small. In short, I would say yes, but only with clear limits.
accepted: To begin with, I would accept the sponsor, because our club needs new equipment and the school cannot pay for it. For instance, the nets are broken, and the balls are old. On balance, I think the benefits outweigh the risks, although I see the dilemma: the café sells sweet drinks, and our club is about health. That said, I would set two conditions. First, the café must also sell water and fruit at our events. Second, the sponsor cannot decide anything about the team. As for your question about the logo, that is a fair point. Let me think for a moment. I would accept a small logo on the shirts, provided that the players agree and the logo stays small. In short, I would say yes, but only with clear limits.

My position is that we should accept the money. The club is small, and it needs new equipment. For example, we have only one good ball, and the shirts are very old. The school cannot pay for new things, so the help of a sponsor is important to us. Although the café sells sweet drinks, we can ask it to offer water as well. That said, I would want a written agreement, because the sponsor should not choose our team. About the logo, good question. Let me think. I would accept it on the shirts, as long as the players agree. I would also ask the players and the families for their opinion before we sign anything. Overall, I would say yes, with clear limits.

feedback.es: Una respuesta completa da la postura, la razón con un ejemplo, un matiz con condiciones y contesta la pregunta inesperada con calma y en la misma estructura.

prompt.es: Redacta un resumen matizado para el ayuntamiento: condición, reserva y plazo.

answer.text: Dear Council, To summarise, the residents of Linden Street have reached a compromise about the empty lot. At first, Mia wanted a garden, whereas Tom wanted parking, but both sides have moved towards the middle. They appear to agree on a small garden on half of the lot, provided that ten parking spaces stay and the garden is open to everyone. Admittedly, one concern remains: some residents fear that weekend noise may increase. Sara has therefore asked for a review in September. On balance, the outcome seems acceptable to most neighbours, although it may not satisfy everyone. We would be grateful if the council could confirm its decision by 15 June. Thank you for your time and attention. Kind regards, The Linden Street residents

Dear Council, In summary, the neighbours of Linden Street have agreed on a compromise for the empty lot. Mia first wanted a garden, while Tom preferred parking, but both have moved a little. A small garden will use half of the lot, as long as ten parking spaces remain and everyone can use the garden. One concern is still open: weekend noise might increase, so Sara has asked for a review in September. Overall, the agreement seems fair to most residents. Please confirm your decision before 15 June, and thank you very much for your time. Yours sincerely, The Linden Street residents
